title: Elysian Finance - workload replay and SLA criteria scoping
summary: POC scoping call to align on workload characterization, replay methodology, success criteria (latency SLOs, throughput, cost targets), and a 4-week benchmark timeline. Discussed QPS/concurrency profiles, input/output token distribution, replay artifacts, and security access. Action items: share replay harness, sample telemetry, schedule infra access, and confirm SLA targets.
topics: Workload replay approach (synthetic vs. production replay)
QPS and burst modeling; concurrency expectations
Input/output token distribution and tail traffic
Latency SLOs and success criteria (p95/p99 targets)
action_items: Maya Patel - provide replay harness (JMeter + python runner) and a small sample dataset - 2026-05-22
Jordan Lee - share anonymized telemetry and a week's traffic sketch (CSV) - 2026-05-21
Carlos Mendes - provide VPC peering checklist and service account for replay runs - 2026-05-24
Alex Chen - send pricing/estimate for dedicated pilot and cost per 1M tokens - 2026-05-20
next_steps: Redwood to ingest sample telemetry and run a baseline replay at low QPS
Customer to approve SSO/KMS access and provide service account for private replay
Schedule hands-on benchmark week (week 3 of POC) and a mid-POC check-in
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-05-19 15:00 UTC; Duration: 48m; Recording: yes; Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Elysian CTO), Priya Nair (PM), Carlos Mendes (Lead SRE)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick intro, I'm Alex with Redwood, AE. Maya is our systems SE who will lead the replay/benchmark side. Could you do quick intros?
[00:10] Jordan Lee: Jordan here, CTO at Elysian. We're running LLMs in a few prod microservices for summaries and question answering across account data. Looking to evaluate Redwood for predictable serving and cost.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Priya, PM on the payments product. Main goals are latency and correctness for real-time customer-facing flows.
[00:24] Carlos Mendes: Carlos, lead SRE. I'll handle infra access and replay plumbing.
[00:30] Maya Patel: Great, today I'd like to align on workload shape — QPS, concurrency, token mix — and define success metrics for the POC. We'll propose a 4-week cadence: week1 telemetry & setup, week2 sizing & config, week3 benchmarking & stress, week4 wrap and decision.
[01:05] Jordan Lee: Sounds good. Quick context — our traffic is hybrid. Most requests are short summarizations with inputs around 40-80 tokens and outputs 80-250 tokens. But we have a long tail: roughly 8-12% of requests are long-form outputs 600-1500 tokens for regulatory exports.
[01:40] Priya Nair: Average QPS across services is about 35, but peak bursts spike up to 420 QPS for short windows — like 30 to 90 seconds during batch runs or end-of-day reports. Concurrency currently varies; we see sustained concurrency around 60 on our busiest instance set.
[02:05] Maya Patel: Helpful. To clarify: average QPS 35, sustained concurrency ~60, burst peaks to ~420 for short periods, long-tail token distribution ~10%. Is that accurate?
[02:12] Jordan Lee: Yes. Also note SLA target for us is p95 < 500ms for interactive flows; for async/regulatory exports we accept higher latency but want throughput guarantees.
[02:30] Alex Chen: Got it. Our typical POC success criteria we recommend: 1) p95 latency under target at defined QPS and concurrency, 2) throughput stability with no errors during bursts, 3) cost estimate within your thresholds, and 4) no quality regressions on your eval set. For Elysian, we should make the p95 target explicit per workload class.
[02:58] Priya Nair: For interactive flows let's aim for p95 < 300ms if possible, but we'll accept up to 500ms initially. For regulatory exports, p99 isn't critical but we want predictable run-times.
[03:15] Maya Patel: Okay we'll architect two benchmark tiers: interactive (low latency) and batch/exports (high throughput). We'll run both model variants — a quantized small-medium under dedicated capacity and a full-precision hosted variant — to measure cost/latency tradeoffs. Note: quantization can change quality slightly; we'll tie that to your eval prompts.
[03:40] Carlos Mendes: Quick question about KV cache and prefix caching — we heavily reuse similar prompts for a subset of flows. Does Redwood support prefix caching or reuse of KV cache between requests to reduce compute?
[03:52] Maya Patel: Yes, Redwood runtime supports KV cache reuse and prefix caching; but to get the best gains we need request patterns that have strong prefix overlap. We'll try a replay with and without cache enabled so you can see the delta. The telemetry you'll share will help quantify that.
[04:20] Jordan Lee: On testing methodology — we'd prefer a mixed approach. Replay real production traces for representative days, plus synthetic stress tests to exercise bursts and long-tail token lengths.
[04:33] Alex Chen: Agreed. Typical replay approach: ingest anonymized request traces (timestamps, prompt hash, input token length, output token length distribution), then run a time-accurate replay that preserves inter-arrival times for baseline. For stress, we do controlled QPS ramps and sustained concurrency tests.
[04:55] Priya Nair: We need to be careful with PII — will scrub and hash prompts. We can provide token lengths and a small sample of prompts if needed.
[05:05] Carlos Mendes: We'll also provide backend SLOs and error budgets. One ask: we use VPC-only egress policies; how does Redwood handle private connectivity?
[05:16] Maya Patel: For Private deployments we support VPC peering and private-hosted control plane options. For hosted POC we can do a secure peered tunnel or use a small dedicated pool in your region. We'll send the VPC checklist.
[05:35] Jordan Lee: Good. Let's quantify the token mix: median input 55 tokens, 75th percentile input 120 tokens, median output 180 tokens, 90th percentile output ~650 tokens, 99th percentile up to 1,400 tokens on rare cases. That matches our export flows.
[06:00] Maya Patel: Those tail numbers matter for batching and kernel selection. We'll need to cap sequence length during some runs to protect runtime memory. For the replay harness, please indicate which requests are allowed to truncate vs require full fidelity.
[06:20] Alex Chen: On metrics we'll capture: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, batch sizes, and error rate. We'll also export cost extrapolations at token-level and per-hour.
[06:33] Priya Nair: What about concurrency mapping? If concurrency is 60 sustained, is that 60 simultaneous decoder steps or 60 in-flight sessions?
[06:44] Maya Patel: In our terms concurrency = in-flight sessions (requests holding a KV cache + decoder). Each session's decode time depends on output length — so long outputs dramatically increase concurrent GPU time. Replay will map decode time to concurrency.
[07:02] Jordan Lee: For the POC timeline, can you outline milestones?
[07:06] Maya Patel: Sure. Week1: telemetry ingestion and infra setup, run a small low-QPS baseline. Week2: sizing, recommend Dedicated capacity options and quantization profiles, configure caching. Week3: full benchmarks — interactive SLA tests and stress burst runs; we'll use both replay and synthetic. Week4: results, cost modeling, decision meeting. We'll include a mid-POC sync at the end of week2.
[07:36] Alex Chen: Also we'll prepare a benchmark sheet with expected token/sec to GPU ratios and recommended concurrency knobs.
[07:45] Carlos Mendes: Who from your side will run the actual benchmark job? Will you run it against our infra or do we initiate runs?
[07:53] Maya Patel: We typically run benchmark orchestrations from a controlled runner — either Redwood-managed in a dedicated project or we provide scripts for your infra. For Private customers we can run the harness inside your VPC using a service account you provide.
[08:08] Jordan Lee: Security review — we need SOC 2 report, KMS integrations, and audit log behavior.
[08:16] Alex Chen: We'll share SOC 2 and ISO artifacts with redactions as needed, plus details on KMS/HSM integrations and per-request audit logs.
[08:28] Priya Nair: On success criteria, let's make it explicit now: interactive flows p95 < 350ms at 40 QPS sustained with concurrency 60; bursts up to 420 QPS for 60-120s with p95 < 800ms. For batch exports, want throughput stability at 2000 concurrent decode threads with no more than 2% error rate and predictable completion times. If Redwood can meet those and cost target (TBD), we'll proceed to a dedicated pilot.
[09:03] Maya Patel: We'll test those SLA points. Two clarifications: 1) for p95 < 350ms, what sequence length are we assuming? 2) for burst window durations, do you expect repeated bursts per hour or isolated events?
[09:17] Jordan Lee: For interactive flows assume average output 180 tokens; burst windows are typically isolated but could happen multiple times a day during settlement periods.
[09:27] Maya Patel: Noted. We'll run a latency matrix varying sequence lengths 64/256/512 tokens to show impact.
[09:36] Carlos Mendes: About replay fidelity — will Redwood replay identical order and timing? We prefer to preserve global timing to test hotspots.
[09:44] Maya Patel: Yes we can do time-accurate replay. We'll also run a shuffled replay to isolate batching sensitivity.
[09:54] Priya Nair: How do we validate quality/regressions? We have a small eval set — about 120 prompts with expected outputs and scoring heuristics.
[10:02] Alex Chen: Perfect — include that eval set. We'll run automated diff-based checks and also sample human checks for long-form. We'll attach quality regression alerts to the POC dashboard so you can see any quality delta from model variant changes.
[10:18] Jordan Lee: Any notes on tokenizer variance and token counting? Our current tokenization uses tiktoken-cl100 but some of our logs miscount when unicode punctuation present.
[10:29] Maya Patel: We'll normalize using the same tokenizer in the replay harness. If you can export raw text and token counts, we'll validate and correct mismatches.
[10:40] Alex Chen: On costs, rough estimate we can provide after initial baseline run. We'll model cost per 1M input+output tokens across hosted vs dedicated with quantization. Expect to deliver a cost delta sheet.
[10:54] Priya Nair: For dedicated capacity, what are typical commit levels you recommend for a pilot? We don't want to overcommit.
[11:05] Maya Patel: For pilots we suggest a small dedicated pool sized to handle your 95th percentile sustained concurrency with headroom for caching gains. We'll propose options: minimal (handles p95 steady), medium (handles steady + small bursts), and large (handles sustained high bursts with autoscale). We'll include burst credits for short windows.
[11:30] Jordan Lee: Timeout and retry behavior — we currently do short retries at the client; does Redwood provide idempotency keys or built-in fallback routing to smaller models when capacity constrained?
[11:41] Maya Patel: We support idempotency and automatic model fallbacks based on routing policies. For strict latency SLOs you can configure immediate fallback to a smaller quantized variant. We'll demo routing rules in the console.
[11:57] Alex Chen: Let's capture instrumentation we'll need: per-request timestamps, token_in, token_out, prompt_hash, status, machine_id. Carlos, can you produce a sample CSV with these columns?
[12:10] Carlos Mendes: Yes we can. I'll scrub PII and produce 48 hours of traffic with sampling. Expect that by Friday.
[12:22] Priya Nair: For the POC evaluation, we also want a cost/capacity sensitivity chart — e.g., how p95 changes as we vary concurrency and batch size.
[12:31] Maya Patel: We'll include a sensitivity matrix in the benchmark report.
[12:38] Jordan Lee: One more: test harness reproducibility. We want to be able to re-run exact experiments. Will Redwood provide reproducible scripts and versions?
[12:48] Maya Patel: Yes — harness, seed values, model versions, and runtime flags will be versioned. We'll push them to a private repo or share via a secure link.
[13:00] Alex Chen: Alright, back to timeline and deliverables: we'll start week1 once you share telemetry and grant access. Mid-week2 we'll present sizing recommendations. Week3 we'll execute benchmarks and deliver a preliminary report within 48 hours after the runs. Week4 final review and contract discussion.
[13:20] Jordan Lee: That aligns. Target start: next Monday (2026-05-25) pending telemetry and access.
[13:27] Alex Chen: Action items recap — Maya will send replay harness, Alex will send cost template and SOC2 artifacts, Jordan/Carlos will share sanitized telemetry and VPC details.
[13:39] Priya Nair: Any blockers from your side?
[13:42] Maya Patel: Nothing, just need the telemetry and a service account.
[13:46] Carlos Mendes: We'll prioritize that. Expect to have the sample trace and service account by 2026-05-21.
[13:53] Jordan Lee: Great, looking forward.
[13:56] Alex Chen: Thanks all. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the mid-POC sync.
[14:05] Maya Patel: I'll also attach the benchmark template and sample replay config to the follow-up email.
[14:12] [meeting ends and recording stops].

Notes / artifacts referenced: replay harness link: https://redwood.example.com/harness/elysian-sample (internal), benchmark spreadsheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d-elysian-bench (customer link placeholder).

Transcription notes: some proper nouns may be mis-transcribed (e.g., KV cache sometimes spoken as "K V cache", VPC as "V P C"). Occasional speaker overlaps and filler words preserved.
